conversation.content: I want to build a website for my business.

Great! Let me start gathering the key information to understand your project.

**What type of business do you have, and what is the primary purpose of the website?** (For example: showcase products, take online orders, provide services, generate leads, etc.)

We run a small landscaping company. The main goal is to showcase our work through photos and projects we've done, and let people contact us to get quotes. Right now we just have a basic Facebook page, so we need something more professional that actually looks like a real business.

Perfect! That's a solid foundation.

**Who is your target audience — are you primarily trying to reach homeowners in your local area, commercial property managers, or both?**

Mostly homeowners in our local area — that's where most of our business comes from. We do some work for property management companies too, but residential is definitely our bread and butter. We're pretty small, so we're not trying to expand beyond our region or anything like that.

Got it. That helps me understand your local focus.

**Do you want customers to be able to book appointments or request quotes directly through the website, or would you prefer they contact you first (via phone, email, or contact form) before scheduling?**

A contact form would be fine — we don't need anything fancy like online booking. We like to talk to customers first anyway to understand what they need before we give them a quote. So just a way for them to reach out with their info and what they're looking for, and then we'll follow up with them.

Makes sense — keeps it personal and lets you qualify leads first.

**Besides the portfolio/gallery of your past projects and a contact form, what other key sections do you think the website needs?** (For example: about your company, services list, testimonials, pricing, team info, etc.)

Yeah, we'd want an about us section so people know a bit about the company and how long we've been around. A services list would be good too — like lawn maintenance, landscaping design, that kind of thing. And if we can get some testimonials or reviews on there, that would help build trust. Pricing... I'm not sure we want to list exact prices since every job is different, but maybe a general idea of what we offer.

That's a smart approach — pricing flexibility makes sense for custom work.

**Do you already have a collection of high-quality photos from past projects that you can use for the portfolio, or do you need help planning how to gather and organize those images?**

We have plenty of photos on our phones and some older ones from jobs we've done over the years. They're not super organized right now, but we've got material to work with. I'd probably need some guidance on what makes good portfolio photos and how to organize them, but we can definitely pull together a decent gallery without having to hire a photographer or anything.

Excellent — you've got the raw materials to work with.

**What's your timeline for getting this website live, and do you have a budget range in mind for the project?**

[DONE]

---

## Requirements Summary

- **Business Type:** Small local landscaping company (residential focus, some commercial)
- **Primary Goals:** Showcase past projects via photo gallery, enable customer contact/quote requests
- **Target Audience:** Local homeowners primarily, with some commercial property managers
- **Key Website Sections:** Portfolio/gallery, About Us, Services list, Testimonials, Contact form
- **Contact/Booking:** Simple contact form only (no online booking) — you'll follow up with customers directly
- **Content:** Have existing photos to use; need guidance on organization and best practices
- **Pricing:** General service descriptions rather than exact pricing due to custom job nature
I need an app that helps people manage their tasks.

Great! I'd like to understand your vision better.

**Who are the primary users of this task management app?** (For example: individual professionals, students, teams within a company, or a specific industry?)

Probably a mix of individual professionals and students, honestly. I use task management myself for work projects and personal stuff, and I know a lot of people around me struggle with staying organized. I'd say my main focus is on individuals who are juggling multiple projects and need something straightforward to keep track of everything.

Perfect, that's helpful context.

**What specific problem are you trying to solve that existing task management apps (like Todoist, Asana, or Microsoft To Do) don't address well?**

Good question. I think most of those apps are either too simple or way too complicated. I want something in the middle — clean and easy to use, but with just enough features to handle priorities and deadlines without feeling overwhelming. A lot of people I talk to say they start using these apps but then abandon them because they're clunky or have too many features they don't need. I want something that actually feels natural to use day-to-day.

That's a clear positioning. I can see the gap you're targeting.

**How do you envision users organizing their tasks — would they primarily work with individual task lists, or do they need to organize tasks across multiple projects?**

I think most people need both, actually. Some tasks are just standalone things — like "call the dentist" — but a lot of people are working on multiple projects at once, whether it's work projects or personal stuff like home renovation or planning a trip. So I'd say they need to group tasks by project, but it shouldn't be mandatory. It should feel flexible enough that you can just add a task quickly without having to set up a whole project structure first.

That makes sense — flexibility is key to avoiding that abandoned-app problem.

**What's your primary monetization strategy — are you thinking free with optional premium features, a subscription model, or something else?**

I'm leaning toward a freemium model, honestly. Keep the core features free so people actually use it and don't abandon it like they do with other apps, but then offer a paid tier for power users who want things like advanced filtering, sharing tasks with others, or maybe integrations with other tools. I think most individual users would be happy with the free version, but teams or people with more complex needs would pay for extra features.

Smart approach — that aligns well with your goal of broad adoption.

**When do you want to launch this, and do you have any constraints on budget, team size, or technology preferences for building it?**

I'm hoping to get an MVP out within the next few months, ideally. As for budget, I have some money set aside but I'm not looking to break the bank — maybe in the $10-15k range to start, so I'd probably need to be lean about it. I don't have a team yet, so I'm thinking I'd either hire a freelancer or a small dev shop to build it. Technology-wise, I'm not too picky — just something that works well on web and mobile and won't be a nightmare to maintain later.

One last thing to nail down scope:

**For your MVP launch, which features are absolutely essential versus which can wait for a later version — for example, is user collaboration/sharing a must-have, or can that come after?**

For the MVP, I just need the basics: creating tasks, organizing them by project, setting due dates and priorities, and being able to check them off when they're done. Maybe a simple search too so people can find tasks quickly. Collaboration and sharing can definitely wait — that's more of a nice-to-have for later. I'd rather launch something solid that one person can use really well than try to do too much and delay getting it out there.

[DONE]

## Requirements Summary

- **Users:** Individual professionals and students juggling multiple projects
- **Core Problem:** Existing task apps are either too simple or too complex; need a "Goldilocks" solution that's intuitive and doesn't feel overwhelming
- **Key Features (MVP):** Task creation, project organization (flexible/optional), due dates, priority levels, task completion, basic search
- **Organization Model:** Support both standalone tasks and project-grouped tasks with flexible workflow
- **Monetization:** Freemium model (free core, paid tier for advanced filtering, sharing, integrations)
- **Timeline & Budget:** MVP within 3 months, ~$10-15k budget
- **Tech Stack:** Web + mobile, maintainable architecture (no specific tech preference given)
- **Launch Scope:** MVP excludes collaboration/sharing features; focus on solid single-user experience first
I want to sell products online.

Great! I'll help you define the requirements for your online store.

**What type of products are you planning to sell?** (For example: physical goods, digital products, services, etc.)
Physical goods, mainly. I'm thinking of starting with apparel and accessories — stuff I can stock and ship out. I might add other things later, but that's where I want to focus initially.

Perfect! That's helpful context.

**Do you already have an existing inventory of apparel and accessories ready to sell, or are you still in the process of sourcing/creating products?**

I'm still working on sourcing. I've got some initial designs and ideas, but I'm still figuring out suppliers and manufacturers. I'm hoping to have a first batch ready in a few months, so I want to get the store up and running soon so I can start taking orders and testing the market.

Understood — you want to be ready to launch before inventory arrives.

**How many different product variations (SKUs) are you expecting to have in your first batch — are we talking dozens, hundreds, or something else?**

I'd say probably in the dozens to start — maybe 30 to 50 different variations across different styles, sizes, and colors. I don't want to overcommit on inventory upfront, so I'm keeping it pretty lean for the launch.

That makes sense for a lean launch.

**Beyond just displaying products and taking payments, what other key features are most important to you?** (For example: customer accounts, email notifications, shipping integrations, analytics, etc.)

Honestly, the basics are what matter most to me right now — I need to be able to process orders and payments smoothly, and I'd like some way to track inventory so I don't oversell. Email notifications would be nice so customers know their order status. As for analytics, I'd like to see which products are selling, but that can probably come later if needed.

Got it — straightforward essentials to start.

**Will you be handling shipping yourself, or are you planning to use a fulfillment service or dropshipper?**

I'll be handling it myself initially — I've got space to store inventory and pack orders. Eventually if things scale up, I might look into a fulfillment service, but for now I want to keep costs down and stay hands-on so I understand the process better.
**What's your timeline for launching the store — are you aiming for a specific date, or just "as soon as possible"?**

As soon as possible, really. I'd like to have something live within the next month or two if we can. I don't have a hard deadline, but I want to get it out there and start testing things with real customers before my inventory arrives.

[DONE]

## Requirements Summary

- **Product Type:** Physical apparel and accessories (30-50 SKUs at launch)
- **Inventory Status:** Still sourcing; first batch expected in a few months
- **Core Features Needed:** Product catalog with variations (styles, sizes, colors), payment processing, inventory management to prevent overselling, order status email notifications
- **Fulfillment:** Self-managed initially (user handles packing/shipping)
- **Analytics:** Basic product sales tracking; detailed analytics can come later
- **Timeline:** Launch within 1-2 months to start market testing before inventory arrives

**Next steps:** You're ready to discuss platform options (Shopify, WooCommerce, custom build, etc.) and begin detailed design/scoping based on these core requirements.
Help me do marketing for my startup.

I'd like to help you scope out a marketing solution. Let me start with the most important question:

**What is your startup's main product or service, and who are your target customers?**

We're building a SaaS platform for small to mid-sized e-commerce businesses to help them manage their inventory and orders across multiple sales channels — like Amazon, Shopify, and their own websites. 

Our target customers are basically shop owners with 5-50 employees who are drowning in spreadsheets and manual work trying to sync everything. They typically make between $500K and $5M in annual revenue.

Great context. That helps clarify the market. Now let me dig into your current situation:

**Where are you in your startup journey right now — are you pre-launch, just launched, or already have paying customers? And if you have customers, roughly how many?**

We're pre-launch right now, so we don't have paying customers yet. We've got a working MVP that we've tested with about 8-10 beta users — mostly friends and contacts in the e-commerce space who've given us good feedback. We're planning to launch publicly in the next 2-3 months, so marketing is kind of urgent for us.

Got it — pre-launch with validated MVP feedback is a solid position. This helps prioritize what we need to focus on.

**Of your 8-10 beta users, how did you initially find or recruit them, and which channels or methods got you the best feedback or strongest interest?**

Honestly, most of them came through personal networks — I reached out to people I knew in the e-commerce space, posted in a couple of Shopify Facebook groups asking for beta testers, and got a few referrals from those initial conversations. 

The Facebook groups actually worked better than I expected — people were pretty eager to jump on a free tool that could solve a real pain point. That's actually part of why I'm here asking for help with marketing now — I want to figure out how to tap into that same kind of interest at scale before we launch.

That's valuable insight — you've already found a channel (Facebook communities) where your customers are actively discussing their pain points. Smart to double down on what's working.

**Before we plan the marketing strategy, what's your primary goal for the 2-3 months leading up to launch — is it to build an email waitlist, generate buzz/awareness, lock in early paying customers, or something else entirely?**

Mainly we want to build an email waitlist — we're aiming for maybe 500-1000 signups before we officially launch so we have people ready to convert on day one. But honestly, if we can lock in some early paying customers during that time, even better. We're not expecting to make huge revenue before launch, but getting some committed users would validate that people will actually pay for this.

Perfect — that's a clear, measurable goal. Knowing you want both waitlist growth AND early paying customers shapes the strategy significantly.

**What's your current marketing budget for the next 2-3 months, and are you planning to do this primarily yourself, hire someone, or use a mix of paid ads and organic outreach?**

We've probably got around $5-10K we could dedicate to marketing over the next couple months, but we're flexible depending on what actually works. Right now it's mostly me handling outreach and content stuff in my spare time since I'm also working on the product, but I know I can't do everything myself at scale.

I'm thinking we'd probably do a mix — like, start with organic stuff since we've had success with that, but use some of the budget for targeted ads or maybe hiring a freelancer to help with content or outreach. I'm just not totally sure what the best way to spend that money would be, which is kind of why I'm here.

Perfect — I have enough to scope this out properly now.

**Last question: Besides Facebook groups, have you identified any other communities, platforms, or channels where your target e-commerce shop owners actively hang out online (Reddit, LinkedIn, Slack communities, industry forums, etc.)?**

Yeah, so I know a lot of them are on Reddit — there's r/ecommerce and r/shopify that seem pretty active. I've also noticed LinkedIn is where some of the slightly larger shop owners tend to be. And there are definitely Slack communities for Shopify sellers, though I haven't dug too deep into those yet.

Honestly, I haven't done a super systematic search for all the places they hang out, so if there are other communities or platforms I'm missing, I'd love to know about them. But those are the main ones I've stumbled across so far.

[DONE]

## Marketing Requirements Summary

**Product & Market:**
- SaaS inventory/order management platform for small-to-mid e-commerce businesses ($500K–$5M revenue, 5–50 employees)
- MVP validated with 8–10 beta users; public launch in 2–3 months

**Primary Goals:**
- Build email waitlist of 500–1,000 signups pre-launch
- Secure early paying customers to validate willingness to pay

**Current State:**
- Pre-launch, no paying customers yet
- Initial traction via personal networks + Shopify Facebook groups (strongest channel so far)
- Marketing budget: $5–10K over 2–3 months
- You handling outreach/content part-time; open to freelance help or paid ads

**Target Channels Identified:**
- Facebook groups (Shopify, e-commerce communities) — proven effective
- Reddit (r/ecommerce, r/shopify)
- LinkedIn (larger shop owner audience)
- Slack communities (Shopify seller groups) — not yet explored

**Next Steps:** You're ready to build a targeted go-to-market strategy leveraging your strongest channel (Facebook) while systematically testing Reddit, LinkedIn, and Slack communities with a mix of organic outreach and paid promotion.
I want a website and some way to get more customers.

Great! I'd like to understand your business better so I can help you build the right solution.

**What type of business or service do you offer?**

We're a local home cleaning service. We've been doing this for a few years now, mostly through word-of-mouth referrals, but we want to grow beyond just our existing clients telling their friends about us.

That makes sense — word-of-mouth is great but you're ready to scale. Let me ask the next critical question:

**Who is your primary target customer?** (For example: busy professionals, families with kids, elderly homeowners, real estate agents, or a mix of different types?)

Mostly busy professionals and young families in our area who don't have time to clean their own homes. We've had some success with real estate agents too — they sometimes need turnover cleans between tenants. I'd say that's probably 70% professionals, 20% families, and 10% real estate stuff, but honestly we take anyone who books us right now.

Perfect, that's helpful. Now I need to understand your current capacity:

**How many cleaning jobs can your team realistically handle per week right now, and do you want to grow that number?**

Right now we're doing maybe 15-20 jobs a week with our current team of three cleaners. We could probably push to 25-30 without hiring anyone else, but honestly we're already getting a bit stretched. I'd like to grow to maybe 40-50 jobs a week, which would mean hiring at least one or two more people.

Got it — you're planning to grow your team too. That's important context.

**What's your budget for building the website and marketing it to get more customers?** (Rough range is fine — for example: $2,000-$5,000 total, $5,000-$10,000, or higher?)

Honestly, I'm not entirely sure what's realistic to spend. I was thinking maybe $3,000 to $5,000 total for everything — the website and getting it in front of people — but I'm open to hearing what you'd recommend. I just don't want to spend a fortune if I'm not sure it'll pay off.

That's a reasonable starting budget. One more critical question before I summarize:

**How do you want customers to book with you?** (For example: should they fill out a form on your website and you call them back, use an online booking calendar where they pick their own time slots, call a phone number, or something else?)

I think an online booking system would be great so people can schedule themselves without having to call me — that'd save me a lot of time. But honestly, I'm not picky as long as people can easily get in touch and book a cleaning. Maybe a form they fill out works too, as long as it's simple for customers.

Perfect — I have what I need. One final question:

**Besides your website and booking system, what's your main concern about getting customers?** (For example: people don't know you exist locally, they don't trust you without seeing reviews, competition from other cleaners, or something else?)

Definitely that people don't know we exist yet. Right now we're basically invisible online — if someone searches for a cleaning service in our area, they won't find us. We need to show up when people are actually looking for what we do. And honestly, reviews would help too since people want to see that other customers trust us before they book.

[DONE]

## Requirements Summary

- **Business:** Local home cleaning service, 3-person team, 15-20 jobs/week currently
- **Target customers:** 70% busy professionals, 20% young families, 10% real estate agents
- **Growth goal:** Scale to 40-50 jobs/week (hiring 1-2 more people)
- **Budget:** $3,000-$5,000 for website + customer acquisition
- **Booking preference:** Online booking system preferred (or simple contact form)
- **Primary challenge:** Lack of online visibility; need to rank locally when people search for cleaning services, plus build social proof through reviews

**Next steps:** You'll need a professional website with local SEO optimization, integrated online booking, a review collection strategy, and a local marketing plan (Google Business Profile, local directories, etc.) to address your main visibility gap.
I want to create an online store for handmade jewelry. I need product pages, a shopping cart, and something for payments. I'd like it to look clean and modern.

Great! I can help you scope this out. Let me start with the most important question:

**Who is your primary target customer, and what's your expected monthly sales volume or number of products you'll launch with?**

(This helps me understand the scale and complexity we're building for — whether this is a side hustle with 50 products or a serious operation with thousands of SKUs.)

Good question. Honestly, I'm starting small — I'm thinking maybe 50 to 100 pieces to launch with, mostly necklaces, bracelets, and earrings that I make myself. As for monthly sales, I don't have a concrete number yet, but I'm hoping to do maybe 10-20 orders a month once I get going. My customers are probably going to be people who appreciate handmade stuff and are willing to pay a bit more for quality — so maybe women aged 25-45 who shop online for unique gifts or personal pieces.

Perfect, that's really helpful context. Now let me ask about the technical side:

**Do you have any preference between using an existing e-commerce platform (like Shopify, WooCommerce, Squarespace) versus building a custom solution from scratch — or are you open to either approach?**

(This matters because it affects timeline, cost, and ongoing maintenance.)

I'm pretty open to either, honestly. I've heard Shopify is easy to use and you don't have to worry about technical stuff, which appeals to me since I'm not super tech-savvy. But if a custom solution would be more affordable long-term or give me more control over the design, I'm interested in hearing about that too. I just want something that doesn't require me to manage a lot of backend stuff — I'd rather focus on making jewelry than troubleshooting the website.

That's a really smart priority. Let me dig into what matters most for your business operations:

**Beyond product pages, shopping cart, and payments, do you need any of these features: order tracking for customers, inventory management to track your stock, email notifications (like order confirmations), or the ability to offer discounts/coupon codes?**

Yeah, those all sound pretty useful actually. Order tracking would be nice so customers know where their stuff is. Inventory management is definitely important since I make everything myself — I need to know what I have in stock so I don't oversell. And email confirmations seem like a no-brainer for customer experience. As for discounts and coupons, maybe down the road, but that's not urgent for launch. I'd rather get the basics right first.

Smart approach. One more key question:

**For payment processing, do you have a preference or requirement — for example, do you want to accept just credit cards, or also digital wallets like PayPal, Apple Pay, and Google Pay?**

Credit cards would be the minimum, definitely. I think PayPal would be good too since a lot of people trust that. As for Apple Pay and Google Pay, I'm not sure if that's necessary to start, but if it's easy to add without extra cost, why not? I just want to make checkout as smooth as possible so people don't abandon their cart at the last second.

Great. Last critical piece:

**What's your timeline and budget for getting this store live — are you thinking weeks, months, or do you have a specific launch date in mind? And do you have a budget range in mind for the initial build?**

Honestly, I'm hoping to launch within the next 2-3 months if possible. I'd like to get it up before the holiday season if I can. As for budget, I'm not entirely sure what's realistic, but I'm thinking somewhere in the $1,000 to $5,000 range for the initial build? I know that's a pretty wide range, but I'm flexible depending on what option makes the most sense. I just don't want to spend a ton upfront since I'm still testing whether this business will actually work.

Perfect, one final clarifying question:

**Will you be handling shipping yourself (printing labels, packing orders), or do you need the store to integrate with a shipping/fulfillment service?**

I'll be handling it myself for now — packing and shipping everything from home. So I don't think I need a full fulfillment service integration right away. But it would be nice if the store could generate shipping labels or at least show me order details clearly so I can print them out and get packages out quickly. Maybe down the road if orders pick up, I'd look into something bigger, but for launching with 10-20 orders a month, I can manage it manually.

[DONE]

## Requirements Summary

**Business & Audience**
- Handmade jewelry store (necklaces, bracelets, earrings)
- Launch with 50-100 products
- Target: Women 25-45 seeking unique, quality pieces
- Expected: 10-20 orders/month initially

**Core Features**
- Product pages with clean, modern design
- Shopping cart
- Payment processing (credit cards + PayPal; Apple/Google Pay optional)
- Order tracking for customers
- Inventory management (critical — no overselling)
- Email order confirmations
- Manual shipping label generation/order details display
- Coupons/discounts: nice-to-have, not urgent for launch

**Technical Approach**
- Preference for low-maintenance, non-technical management
- Open to Shopify or custom solution; prioritizes ease of use over extensive customization
- No need for fulfillment service integration yet

**Timeline & Budget**
- Launch target: 2-3 months (before holiday season)
- Budget: $1,000-$5,000 for initial build
- Flexible based on business viability

---

**Next step:** I'd recommend evaluating **Shopify** (fastest/lowest risk for 2-3 month timeline, ~$30-300/month ongoing) vs. a **lightweight custom build** (higher upfront cost but lower monthly fees). Both fit your needs perfectly.
I'm building a SaaS tool for small accounting firms. It should let them track client invoices, send reminders, and generate monthly reports. I want a subscription model.

Great! I can see the core functionality and business model. Let me start gathering the critical details.

**Who are your primary users within these accounting firms?** (e.g., firm owners, office managers, accountants, or a mix?) This will help me understand the user experience requirements.

Good question. Honestly, it's probably a mix, but I'd say the primary users would be office managers and junior accountants who handle the day-to-day invoice stuff. They're the ones actually sending reminders and chasing payments. The firm owners would use it mainly to check reports and see how things are going overall, but they're not in there every day.

Perfect context. That helps clarify the user personas.

**How many clients would a typical accounting firm need to manage invoices for?** (e.g., are we talking 10-50 clients, hundreds, or varies widely?) This affects scalability and UI complexity.

It varies a lot, but from what I've talked to some smaller firms, they're usually managing somewhere between 20 to 100 clients. A few of the bigger ones might go higher, but I'm really targeting the smaller end of the market initially — so I'd say plan for at least up to 100 or maybe 150 to be safe. That's the sweet spot where they still need better organization but aren't so massive that they need enterprise-level solutions.

Excellent — that's a solid scope boundary.

**For your subscription pricing model, are you planning tiered plans** (e.g., basic/pro/enterprise based on features or user count), **or a single flat-rate plan?** This affects how you'll structure access and features.

I think tiered makes more sense. Maybe a basic plan for solo practitioners or really small firms — just the core invoice tracking and reminder stuff. Then a pro tier with the monthly reports and maybe some additional features like custom templates or client portals. I haven't locked in exact pricing yet, but tiering lets us capture different segments without building completely different products.

Smart approach — tiering gives you good upsell potential.

**When you mention "monthly reports," what specific data or metrics do these need to show?** (e.g., outstanding invoices, payment trends, revenue by client, aging reports, or something else?)

Yeah, so things like total outstanding invoices, which clients are overdue, and maybe revenue breakdown by client month-over-month. An aging report would be useful too — like showing invoices that are 30, 60, 90 days overdue. Basically, the firm owner wants to quickly see the health of cash flow and which clients aren't paying on time. I don't need anything super complex at first, just enough to give them the quick snapshot they're after.

That's a clear picture of the reporting needs.

**Do you need to integrate with any existing accounting software** (like QuickBooks, Xero, FreshBooks, etc.), **or will firms be manually entering/uploading invoice data into your platform?**

Good point. I think manual entry is fine to start — it keeps things simpler to build and launch faster. But yeah, QuickBooks integration would be nice down the road since a lot of these firms already use it. That said, I don't want to get blocked on integrations right now. If we can get the core product working well with manual data entry, we can add connectors later when we have more resources.

Perfect — that's a pragmatic phased approach.

**What's your target launch timeline, and do you have any constraints on budget or team size for building this?** This helps me understand if we're looking at MVP in 2 months with a small team, or a more extended build.

I'm hoping to launch something basic within 3-4 months ideally. Budget-wise, I've set aside maybe $15-20K to get started, so I need to be smart about it — probably a freelancer or small agency rather than a full in-house team. I know that's tight, so we'd need to focus on just the essentials for launch: invoice tracking, basic reminders, and simple monthly reports. The bells and whistles can come later once we validate the market.

[DONE]

## Requirements Summary

- **Users:** Office managers & junior accountants (day-to-day); firm owners (reporting/oversight)
- **Scale:** 20-150 clients per firm initially
- **Core Features:** Invoice tracking, automated payment reminders, monthly cash flow reports (outstanding totals, overdue aging by 30/60/90 days, revenue by client)
- **Pricing:** Tiered model (Basic: core tracking/reminders; Pro: reports + templates + client portals)
- **Data Entry:** Manual initially; QuickBooks integration deferred to Phase 2
- **Timeline:** MVP launch in 3-4 months
- **Budget & Team:** ~$15-20K, likely freelancer/small agency
- **MVP Scope:** Invoice tracking, basic reminders, simple monthly reports only

**Next steps:** Define exact feature priorities, create wireframes for the office manager workflow, and scope the database/API structure to support tiered access.
I need a website for my restaurant in Paris. It should show the menu, allow table reservations, and have a contact page. We post a lot on Instagram so maybe something for that too.

Great! I'll help you scope this out efficiently.

**What is your primary goal for this website** — is it mainly to drive reservations, showcase your cuisine to attract new customers, or something else?

I'd say it's mostly to drive reservations, honestly. We get a lot of walk-ins, but having an easy way for people to book tables online would save us time and reduce phone calls. That said, we definitely want it to look good since so many people check us out online first — so showcasing the food and atmosphere is important too.

Makes sense — reservations and visual appeal are both key.

**How many tables does your restaurant have, and what's your typical seating capacity per service?** (This will help determine if you need a simple booking system or something more sophisticated for managing availability.)

We have about 30 tables, so we can seat around 100 people per service. We do lunch and dinner, so there's some turnover, but nothing crazy. I think a simple booking system should work fine — we're not so big that we need something super complex. As long as people can pick a date, time, and party size, we should be good.

Perfect — that's helpful context.

**Who will be managing the reservations on your end** — do you have someone checking the bookings regularly, or do you need the system to automatically send confirmations and reminders to customers?

One of my managers handles most of the reservations during the day, but honestly, they're pretty busy. Automatic confirmations and reminders would be really helpful — that way customers get reminded and we don't have as many no-shows. It would definitely make things easier for the team.

Understood — automation will save your team time and reduce no-shows.

**For your menu, do you change it seasonally, monthly, or do you keep it fairly consistent?** (This affects how often you'll need to update the website and what kind of content management system would work best for you.)
